name: Video tape recorder
effect: atoms are tiny magnets
how: A tape recorder fast enough for television. A spinning electromagnet head lines up the tiny atomic magnets in a coated plastic tape, so the picture is kept as a trail of magnetized spots that can be played back the same evening.

name: Hard disk drive
effect: atoms are tiny magnets
how: A computer's long-term memory. A head floating a hair's width above a spinning platter flips the direction of tiny magnetized patches, one bit each, and they keep their direction with the power off.

name: Memory chip (DRAM)
effect: static charge
how: The working memory of every computer. Each bit is a small electric charge parked on a microscopic capacitor next to a transistor switch. The charge leaks away, so the chip tops it up thousands of times a second.

name: Flash memory
effect: quantum tunnelling
how: Memory that keeps its data with the power off, used in phones, cameras and USB sticks. Because electrons are also waves, a strong voltage lets them pass straight through a thin insulator onto an isolated 'floating gate', where they stay trapped for years.

name: Giant magnetoresistance read head
effect: a thin magnetic layer changes a current's resistance
how: The sensor that let hard disks grow a hundredfold. A stack of metal layers a few atoms thick changes its electrical resistance sharply when a tiny magnetized bit passes underneath, so much smaller bits can still be read.

name: Personal computer
how: A whole computer for one person on a desk. A single microprocessor chip does the work, a keyboard and mouse take input, and an ordinary TV screen shows the result. It works by the same logic as the room-sized computers before it, so it is an improvement, not a new principle.
revision: Added the computer mouse as a part (Boris's note, r10).

name: Deep neural network
effect: a web of simple cells learns by strengthening its connections
how: Software that learns to recognize speech, faces and words from examples instead of rules. It copies the brain's plan: layers of simple units, like nerve cells, pass signals along connections whose strengths are nudged after every mistake until the answers come out right.
revision: Effect card is now Neuron theory (1889), per r8.

name: Public-key cryptography
effect: multiplying primes is easy, factoring is hard
how: Lets two strangers talk secretly over an open line, which is how every web purchase is protected. Anyone can lock a message with the public key, a huge number made by multiplying two primes; only someone who knows those two primes can unlock it, and finding them from the product would take longer than the age of the universe.
effectCardNew: Every whole number is a unique product of primes, and there is no end of primes. Multiplying two big primes is quick; finding them again from the product is hopelessly slow.
revision: Proposes a new card, Prime numbers. The board already counts math as an effect (microchips work by Boolean logic and binary numbers).

name: Computer mouse
effect: a rolling ball grips the surface instead of sliding
how: A pointer you move by hand. A rubber ball underneath grips the desk and rolls rather than slides, turning two small wheels at right angles, so the computer can count how far the hand moved left-right and up-down.
revision: Narrower effect (r11): the ball grips and rolls instead of sliding.

name: Capacitive touchscreen
effect: static charge
how: A screen you point at with a finger, as on every phone. A grid of transparent electrodes under the glass holds a small charge; a fingertip, which conducts, draws some of it away, and the chip finds the spot where the charge dropped.

name: Barcode scanner
effect: black stripes soak up light, white gaps reflect it
how: Reads a price at the checkout in a blink. A laser spot sweeps across printed stripes, and a photocell turns the flicker of reflected light, strong from the white gaps and weak from the black bars, into a number the computer looks up.
revision: Narrower effect (r11): black bars soak up light while white gaps reflect it. Borderline: it may really be an improvement.

name: CCD image sensor
effect: photoelectric effect
how: The chip that replaced film in cameras and telescopes. Light falling on each pixel knocks electrons loose, so the brighter the spot the more charge collects; the charges are then shuffled out row by row and counted.

name: MP3 audio compression
effect: the ear misses quiet sounds next to loud ones
how: Shrinks recorded music about tenfold, which made music downloads and the iPod possible. The ear can't hear a quiet sound right next to a loud one in pitch or time, so the encoder simply throws those sounds away.

name: Liquid crystal display
effect: lined-up liquid crystals twist light, and a voltage untwists them
how: The flat screen of watches, laptops and TVs. A film of liquid crystal sits between two crossed polarizing sheets; its molecules twist the light so it gets through, and a small voltage straightens them so that dot goes dark.
effectCardNew: Some substances flow like a liquid while their long molecules stay lined up like a crystal; an electric field or a flow can swing them all round together.
revision: Proposes a new card, Liquid crystals (1888), shared with Kevlar.

name: Electronic paper
effect: charged particles move through a solution
how: The paper-like screen of e-book readers, easy to read in sunlight. Each dot is a tiny capsule of clear fluid holding charged black and white grains; a voltage pulls one colour to the top, and it stays there with no power at all.

name: Packet-switched network
how: The way the Internet carries everything. Messages are cut into small addressed packets that travel separately by whatever route is free and are put back together at the end, so no line is tied up and a broken link is simply routed around. Claude now counts it as an improvement: the idea is a design, not a principle of nature.
revision: Now an improvement: the idea is a network design, not a principle of nature.

name: World Wide Web
how: Pages on any computer in the Internet, linked so a click on one opens another anywhere in the world. It runs on the network that already existed; what it added was the link and the browser, not a new principle.

name: Cellular phone
how: A telephone you carry. It is a small two-way radio that talks to the nearest tower, and as you move, the call is handed from one tower's area, or cell, to the next. Radio already did this job, so it is an improvement.

name: Smartphone
how: A phone, camera, map, music player and computer behind one touchscreen. Every piece was already invented; putting them in a pocket changed daily life more than most inventions.
revision: Added the touchscreen as a part (r10).

name: Ultrasound scanner
effect: sound echoes off the boundaries between soft tissues
how: Lets doctors see inside the body without X-rays, most famously the unborn child. A probe sends pulses of very high-pitched sound and listens for the faint echoes from every boundary between organs; the timing of each echo places it on a screen.
revision: Narrower effect (r11): echoes off the boundaries between soft tissues.

name: MRI scanner
effect: atomic nuclei in a magnet answer radio waves
how: Takes detailed pictures of soft tissue like the brain, with no radiation. In a very strong magnet the hydrogen nuclei in the body's water all line up; a radio pulse tips them over, they ring back with faint radio signals, and a computer works out where each signal came from.

name: PET scanner
effect: matter meets antimatter and vanishes into two gamma rays
how: Shows which parts of the body are busy, such as a working brain region or a growing tumour. The patient is given sugar tagged with an atom that gives off positrons; each positron meets an electron and both vanish into two gamma rays flying in opposite directions, and detectors that catch both at once draw a line through the spot.
revision: Dropped the cyclotron (it makes the tracer elsewhere, per Boris's note and r9); effect card is now Positron (1932), per r8.

name: Pulse oximeter
effect: blood turns bright red when it carries oxygen
how: The clip on a patient's finger that shows how much oxygen their blood carries. Blood rich in oxygen is bright red and blood without it is dark, so the clip shines red and infrared light through the fingertip and compares how much of each gets through.
revision: Effect card is now Blood colors (1669), per Boris's note and r8.

name: Cochlear implant
effect: nerve signals are electrical
how: Gives hearing to people who are profoundly deaf. A microphone and chip split sound into pitches, and a row of electrodes threaded into the inner ear gives tiny shocks to the hearing nerve at the right places, which the brain learns to hear as sound.

name: Oral rehydration salts
effect: the gut pulls in salt and water along with sugar
how: A drink that keeps people with cholera and other diarrhoea alive; it has saved tens of millions of lives. The gut can't absorb plain water fast enough during cholera, but sugar and salt together drag water in with them.

name: Monoclonal antibodies
effect: each immune cell makes one antibody that fits one target
how: Drugs that seek out one exact target, used against cancers and autoimmune disease. Each immune cell makes only one kind of antibody; fusing such a cell with a cancer cell, which never dies, gives a culture that turns out that one antibody for ever.
revision: Effect card is now Vaccination, as Boris suggested; effect restated as one cell, one antibody.

name: PCR
effect: DNA strands part when heated and pair again when cooled
how: Copies a chosen stretch of DNA a billionfold in an afternoon, used in forensics, research and COVID tests. Heating splits the double helix into single strands; on cooling, an enzyme from hot-spring bacteria builds each strand back into a pair, doubling the DNA every cycle.

name: DNA sequencing
effect: parts of a mixture travel at different speeds
how: Reads the letters of a gene, and later of the whole human genome. Copies of the DNA are made that stop at each letter, and the pieces are pulled through a gel, where shorter ones travel faster, so their order spells out the sequence.

name: CRISPR gene editing
effect: bacteria cut the DNA of viruses that match a stored guide
how: Edits a chosen gene in almost any living thing, cheaply and precisely. Bacteria defend themselves against viruses by keeping snippets of viral DNA and cutting any DNA that matches; given a guide of our choosing, the same cutting enzyme goes wherever we send it.
revision: Effect card is now Bacteriophages (1915), per r8.

name: mRNA vaccine
effect: a cell follows genes put into it
how: The COVID vaccines that were designed in days. Instead of a weakened virus, the shot carries the genetic message for one viral protein wrapped in a bubble of fat; the body's own cells read it, make the protein, and the immune system learns to recognize it.

name: Laser eye surgery
effect: ultraviolet light breaks bonds without heating
how: Corrects short sight so people can stop wearing glasses. Pulses of ultraviolet laser light break the bonds holding the cornea's molecules together without heating the tissue around them, reshaping its curve a fraction of a micron at a time.

name: Radioisotope thermoelectric generator
effect: a temperature difference between two metals drives a current
how: A nuclear battery with no moving parts, powering Voyager and the Mars rovers for decades. A lump of plutonium stays hot from its own radioactivity, and rows of thermocouples, junctions of two different metals, turn the difference between that heat and cold space directly into electric current. Its main part, the thermocouple, isn't on the board yet.
revision: Its main part, the thermocouple, isn't on the board, so it's missing a part.

name: Wind turbine
effect: lift
how: The tall three-bladed towers of wind farms. Each blade is a long wing, so the wind gives it lift that pulls it around, rather than just pushing as on an old windmill; the rotor turns a generator through a gearbox.
revision: Borderline: the windmill already did this job, so the new thing is a blade that works by lift instead of drag.

name: Lithium-ion battery
effect: lithium ions slip between layers of carbon
how: The rechargeable battery in phones, laptops and electric cars. Lithium ions slip in between the layers of a graphite electrode when charging and move back to a metal-oxide one when in use, so neither electrode is eaten away and the battery lasts thousands of cycles.

name: Superconducting magnet
effect: some metals lose all resistance when very cold
how: The powerful magnets inside MRI scanners and particle accelerators. Coils of special wire, cooled by liquid helium to a few degrees above absolute zero, lose all electrical resistance, so they carry enormous currents with no heat and no power once started.

name: LED lighting
how: White LED bulbs that use a tenth of the power of a filament bulb. A blue LED shines on a yellow phosphor coating and together they look white. LEDs already made light the same way, so this is an improvement.

name: Microwave oven
effect: water molecules soak up microwaves and heat up
how: Heats food in a minute or two. A magnetron fills the box with microwaves, which water molecules soak up by jiggling back and forth billions of times a second, so the food heats from the inside while the plate stays cool.
revision: Narrower effect (r11): water soaking up microwaves, not just 'radio waves', which the magnetron already has.

name: Induction cooktop
effect: currents stirred up inside a metal heat it
how: A stove top that heats the pan but not itself. A coil under the glass makes a rapidly changing magnetic field, which stirs up swirling currents inside the iron pan, and the pan's own resistance turns them into heat.
revision: Narrower effect (r11): currents stirred up inside the pan heat it, not just 'induction', which the transformer already has.

name: Catalytic converter
effect: catalysis
how: The box in a car's exhaust that removes most of its poisons. Hot exhaust passes over a ceramic honeycomb coated with platinum, which speeds up the reactions that turn carbon monoxide, unburned fuel and nitrogen oxides into carbon dioxide, water and nitrogen, without being used up itself.

name: Reverse-osmosis desalination
effect: small molecules seep through a membrane
how: How most of the world's desalination plants make drinking water from the sea. A thin plastic membrane lets water molecules through but not salt; normally water would flow toward the salty side, but pushing the sea water hard enough forces it the other way.

name: Hovercraft
effect: compressed gas pushes back
how: A craft that travels over water, mud, sand or ice alike. A fan blows air under the hull, where a rubber skirt holds it in; the trapped air is squeezed and pushes back hard enough to lift the craft off the surface, so there is almost no friction.

name: Maglev train
effect: like magnetic poles push apart
how: A train that floats a centimetre above its track, reaching 600 km/h. Electromagnets on the train and in the guideway are set so that their poles repel or attract just enough to hold it up with no wheels, and a magnetic field that travels along the track pulls it forward.
revision: Narrower effect (r11): like poles push apart, card Magnetic pole (1269).

name: Quadcopter drone
effect: a heavy mass stays put while the ground moves
how: The small four-rotor drone. It has no tail and no moving controls; a chip-sized sensor feels the tiniest tilt because a tiny weight inside it lags behind, and the chip speeds up or slows each rotor hundreds of times a second to stay level.

name: Ionization smoke detector
effect: radiation ionizes what it passes through
how: The cheap ceiling alarm found in most homes. A speck of radioactive americium knocks electrons off air molecules, so a small current flows across a gap; smoke particles soak up the charged molecules, the current drops, and the alarm sounds.

name: Airbag
effect: burns all at once, without air
how: A cushion that bursts out of the steering wheel in a crash. A sensor fires a pellet of propellant that carries its own oxygen, so it burns all at once and fills a nylon bag with gas in about thirty thousandths of a second.

name: Kevlar
effect: lined-up rod-like molecules make a fibre as strong as its bonds
how: The fibre in bulletproof vests, five times stronger than steel for its weight. Its molecules are stiff rods that line up by themselves in a liquid-crystal solution, and spinning the solution into a fibre freezes them in line, so a pull is taken by the strong bonds along every molecule.
effectCardNew: Some substances flow like a liquid while their long molecules stay lined up like a crystal; an electric field or a flow can swing them all round together.
revision: Proposes a new card, Liquid crystals (1888), shared with the LCD. The way it works is confirmed.

name: Thermal imaging camera
effect: heat radiates as invisible light
how: Sees people, animals and hot engines in total darkness or smoke, used by firefighters and soldiers. Everything warm gives off infrared light, the warmer the brighter; a special lens and sensor chip turn that invisible glow into a picture.

name: Laser rangefinder
effect: signal delay gives distance
how: Measures distance by timing light, from surveyors' tools to the distance to the Moon. A laser fires a short pulse, a photocell catches its reflection, and since light's speed is known exactly, the round-trip time gives the distance, to within centimetres even off mirrors left on the Moon.

name: Gravitational-wave detector
effect: a passing gravitational wave stretches space
how: Hears colliding black holes across the universe. Two four-kilometre arms at right angles carry laser beams back and forth; a passing gravitational wave stretches one arm and squeezes the other by a thousandth of a proton's width, and the light waves fall out of step.

name: Scanning tunnelling microscope
effect: quantum tunnelling
how: The first microscope to show single atoms. A needle with a one-atom tip is held just above a surface; electrons tunnel across the gap, and the current changes so sharply with distance that tracking it maps every atom's bump.

name: Atomic force microscope
effect: elasticity
how: Maps surfaces atom by atom, even ones that don't conduct, like living cells. A tiny springy arm with a sharp tip is dragged across the surface and bends as it feels each atom; a laser bounced off the arm shows how far it bent.

name: Inkjet printer
effect: piezoelectricity
how: The everyday home printer. Behind each of hundreds of tiny nozzles a crystal flexes when given a voltage and squirts out a droplet of ink, thousands of times a second, while motors step the head across the page and feed the paper.
revision: Added electric motors for moving the head and paper (Boris's note).

name: 3D printer
effect: ultraviolet light hardens a liquid resin
how: Builds a solid object straight from a computer drawing. An ultraviolet laser traces one thin slice of the object on the surface of a liquid plastic, which hardens wherever the light falls; the platform sinks a little and the next slice is drawn on top.
revision: Effect card is now Ultraviolet (1801), per r8.
